title: Gateless Barrier, Case 46: Proceed From the Top of the Pole
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Mumonkan case 46, "Proceed From the Top of the Pole," and traces it to its longer source, Book of Serenity case 79, where Changsha sends a monk to ask his Dharma brother Hui about life before and after meeting Nanquan. Hui's answer, "There couldn't be anything else," becomes a phrase Nomon invites listeners to feel in body and heart. Nomon imagines the pole as a comfortable platform and links stepping off it to the sangha leaving its building on Saturday, with Dogen's backward step as another way to picture the leap. Nomon closes with Wumen's verse against drawing another's bow, riding another's horse, or discussing another's faults, and the memory of forty-something people walking slowly up Laurel Street.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed, penetrating, and perfect dharma is rarely met with even a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the tathagata's words.*
Good evening everybody.
You hear the rain pounding down on my little skylights here?
I had trouble.
And happy solstice, I mean equinox, happy equinox.
That little dedication came to us from San Francisco Zen Center via Dublin, Ireland, oddly enough.
I was corresponding a little bit on one of the Zen priest lists with a priest named Myozan, who runs a little sangha like ours in Dublin, called Zen Buddhism Ireland.
He mentioned that their Tuesday night sit was Tuesday at 8 GMT, and I thought, huh, that's today at noon.
I could do that.
I haven't taken much advantage of the Zoom thing.
I know some of you have more than me.
But from noon to two yesterday, Tuesday, I actually spent the evening in Dublin.
He was very welcoming, and he did a little service with the Heart Sutra in Japanese.
He did that echo for the autumnal equinox in a charming Irish accent, which I won't attempt.
So that was nice.
And little did I know what I was getting myself in for.
When it was time for the discussion at the end, he introduced me and I introduced myself, very friendly.
And then he says, so I'll try as I can a little bit, "Okay, Tim, would you give the talk next week?"
And I said, "Oh, okay.
Yes."
So anyway, if you're interested, email me and I'll send you the link if you want to spend next Tuesday night in Dublin, which is actually Tuesday at noon here.
I'll give the talk and you can meet the charming Zen students of Dublin and hear their accents.
They all go by Japanese names, too, so it's all very confusing.
Nice guy, though.
It's funny: I said, "Wow, what a brilliant echo.
Where'd you get that?"
And he said San Francisco.
I said, "Oh, that's my lineage."
Anyway, Mumonkan case 46 is surprisingly apt to the timing, given what we decided to do and what we did do on Saturday.
Case 46.
Proceed from the top of the pole.
How about that, huh?
*Zen Master Shershuang said, when standing at the top of a hundred foot pole, one more step is necessary.
Another eminent teacher of old said, you who sit at the top of a hundred foot pole, although you have entered the way, you are not yet genuine.
Proceed from the top of the pole, and you will show your whole body in the ten directions.*
That's case 46.
*Zen Master Shershuang said, when standing at the top of a hundred foot pole, one more step is necessary.
Another eminent teacher of old said, you who sit at the top of a hundred foot pole, although you have entered the way, you are not yet genuine.
Proceed from the top of the pole, and you will show your whole body in the ten directions.*
This case has a sort of layering that's not uncommon in koan literature.
There are two different parts which happen at two different times.
A featured teacher here, Shershuang, is talking to his students and he brings up the story of the hundred foot pole.
Shershuang says, when you're standing there, don't just stand there, one more step is necessary, which means you're going to step off, right?
And then, I don't know if it was Shershuang or Master Wu Men who collected these, but I suspect Wu Men adds more, you know?
The more is the little bit longer story from earlier.

"Another eminent teacher of old said, you who sit"—not stand but sit—"you who sit on the top of the pole, although you have entered the way, you are not yet genuine, proceed from the top of the pole and you will show your whole body, show your whole body in the ten directions."
So it turns out there's an even longer story.
The second part is an excerpt from another koan, so it's layers and layers.
The longer koan is in the Book of Serenity koan collection, called Shouyu Roku in Japanese, and it's case 79 there.
Here we find out who this eminent teacher of old was.
He wasn't named in our case tonight.
His name was Master Changsha.
So here's the older koan that the our one got extracted from.
*Changsha had a monk ask Master Hui, "How was it before you saw Nanquan?"
Hui remained silent.
The monk said, "How about after seeing him?"
Hui said, "There couldn't be anything else."
The monk returned and related this to Changsha.
Changsha said, "The man sitting atop a hundred foot pole, though he's gained entry, this is not yet genuine.
Atop the hundred foot pole he should step forward.
The universe, in all directions, is the whole body."
And then the monk said, "Atop the hundred foot pole, how can you step forward?"
Changsha said, "The mountains of Long, the rivers of Li."
The monk said, "I do not understand."
Changsha said, "The whole land is under imperial sway."*
Got all that?
The longer ones are hard, you know, especially if you're not looking at the text.
So I'll read it in while I unpack it a bit.
This is Book of Serenity, case 79, which is where Mumonkan on case 46 comes from, apparently.
There are three characters: Changsha, Hui, and an unnamed monk.
A little backstory helps, actually.
Masters Hui and Changsha are Dharma brothers, and this story is set at the monastery where they're both now practicing as senior monks.
Changsha is the abbot, and his Dharma brother Hui decided to go practice on his own in a hermitage up above on the mountain.
The hermitages are always up above on the mountain.
That's where they go.
It's nicely ambiguous, the way the story is presented, which is better, you know?
Because they're peers, really.
They both studied under another famous teacher, Nan Chuan.

So it's ambiguous whether Master Changsha made a good choice by being abbot and running the place, being the teacher, or Master Hui made a better decision practicing on his own in a hermitage with no one else around, no structure, his own schedule, making his practice his home, or his home his practice.
Their shared teacher, Nan Chuan, there's a million stories about him.
He's the Polishing the Tile guy, and a teacher of Zhaozhou.
There's a small set of legendary figures, and Nan Chuan is one of those.
He's in the case that we used for the Shuso ceremony, about everyday mind is the way, so he's all over the place.
He gets mentioned in the story.
And the monk is a younger monk of some kind, no name.
Okay, so that's the backstory.
Here's the case again from Book of Serenity.
*Changsha had a monk ask Master Hui*, so go up to his hermitage, *"How was it before you saw Nan Chuan?"* And Hui Mi remained silent.

And so the monk said, *"How about after seeing him?"* And Hui said, *"There couldn't be anything else."* *The monk returned and related this to Changsha.* And then Changsha, to the assembled monks, we assume, these things often happen in Dharma talks: *"The man sitting atop the 100 foot pole, though he's gained entry, this is not yet genuine.
Atop the 100 foot pole he should step forward.
The universe in all directions is the whole body."*
We won't worry about the end part.
So Changsha is responding.
He sent this monk up to check on his friend at the hermitage, and then he responds with this verse that became itself a koan.
Let's look at the interaction between the monk and Master Hui up at the hermitage, because it's pretty interesting.
The monk asks on Changsha's behalf, how was it before you saw Nan Chuan?
In other words, what was your life like before you met your teacher?
Before you practiced in this way?
Or if you want to be a little dualistic, what was your life like before enlightenment?
And Hui answered in a great Zen way: just sat zazen, didn't say anything.
Life before his teacher is about silence, or that's the way he presented that life.
So the monk persists.
He wants to be able to tell his teacher, Changsha, something.
He asks what about after seeing him?
What about after your training?
What about after enlightenment?
What about after seeing more clearly?
And I really appreciate Hui's statement.
I think we can practice with this.
There couldn't be anything else.
There couldn't be anything else.
So just feel into that for a minute.
You can close your eyes if you want.
How does it land in your body and your heart to really feel that and say that to yourself?
There couldn't be anything else.
It's interesting, huh?
And it's really practical, right?
We can apply that teaching.
There's some depth there that we can apply to our lives and to the situation, to the world.
Especially maybe when we're agitated and we wish it was some other way.
Ah, there couldn't be anything else.
Right?
It all came together like this.

Another way of saying this is "this is it," or all the different Zen phrases, but it's good for us to have different words for exploration of this radical suchness of everything, the isness of everything, like here it is.
It doesn't mean it's all hunky-dory with us if there's violence and confusion and conflict, but there couldn't be anything else.
And then what?
So you might take that up in your practice a little bit.
There couldn't be anything else.
Also in peaceful times, listening to the rain, right?
There couldn't be anything else.
So the monk goes back down and reports back.
Here's what your old friend told me.
First he didn't tell me anything.
He was silent and then he told me this: there couldn't be anything else.
So Changsha is sending a message back.
*This man sitting atop the 100-foot pole*, being Master Hui, *though he's gained entry, this is not yet genuine.
Atop the 100-foot pole he should step forward.
The universe in all directions is the whole body.* And probably this is also a reference to something else, some ancient Chinese poem or yet another koan, but I don't know.
I didn't try to figure that out.
But it's interesting because it's a verse or a statement of both approval and encouragement.
I think we've heard that every time in these koans, right?
There's encouragement to go deeper, but sometimes it's hard to hear the approval.
Sometimes these guys sound a bit brusque, very critical.
Maybe that's partly just how we hear things, because aren't we always running around worried about getting criticized, basically?
Even if we hear a lot of encouragement and approval, it's like, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, when's the other foot going to fall?
There's some psychology about that.
It's called the negativity bias of the brain.
Great.
That's also something we can train in.
We can train in feeling the encouragement.
And even in the criticism, there's more encouragement, too, right?
So, dear brother, you're sitting atop the 100-foot pole.
You've gained entry.
You've gained entry.
That's a powerful statement.
But it's not yet genuine, right?
Not yet completely entered into, embodied.
I think he's talking about us.
Don't you think?
We've all practiced, some of us for a very long time.
We found our way of doing our life, and probably over time there's more balance and more poise, you know?
Less reactivity.
We can sit atop the 100-foot pole.
We've gained entry.
But something's not yet, right?
Something not quite.
Some way we haven't fully brought this home.
For me lately, I was inspired when we had my friend from Portland, Kakemyo Kum.
He was talking about using mantras and little practices at home all the time.
I never really took that up until just recently.
Just recently I've been offering incense and bowing before bed and doing some chanting.
I don't know why I always relegated that to the center for some reason.
I mean, I've always sat at home.
So there are so many ways we can become a little more genuine, which is a little loaded, but you know what I mean.
Enter more fully.
Be more completely here, whether that has a look of formal practice or just the feel of being a little more fully ourselves.
And it does work.
So Master Changsha makes this recommendation for his friend and thus for us also.
*Atop the hundred-foot pole, step forward.

The universe in all directions is the whole body.* Whatever degree of comfort and balance we've created in our lives, whether we attribute that to practice or just persistence or dumb luck, or whatever sense of progress we feel in our quest to be ourselves and not be suffering all the time, maybe there's a way that it's just like building this platform on top of a pole, trying to make it comfortable, very nice.
And that does pretty well.
But don't you think it's time to go further, to not just rest there?
Don't you think this practice and this life and this world have much deeper potential than some modicum of, more or less, acceptance and comfort we've managed so far, or I've managed?
I don't want to speak for you.
I like this metaphor.
It doesn't say this in the story, but I came up with it: it's pretty uncomfortable on top of a pole, so we built a nice platform, right?
I mean, it's lofty, and it requires balance and care.
We've got to balance our life very carefully.
Even if we build a nice platform, it's still not so easy to stay up there.
But maybe it's time to step off.
That is a little of what we did collectively as a sangha by leaving our building so powerfully on Saturday.
But at first it sounds crazy, right, which is how that idea sounded to every single one of us, including me, when I thought of it.
Like, what?
Leave our place?
We love this place.
Leave the comfort of our platform?
Leave our home?
Becoming a monk is called becoming a home-leaver.
In our tradition, we still stay in homes, but we can internally cultivate that quality of being a home-leaver, of stepping off.
I think it's just like Dogen's idea of taking the backward step, and maybe that'd be even better.
Not stepping forward, so you think you can see where you're going, even though really you can't, right, because there's infinite space there.
And you don't know if there's a bottom.
You don't know what it will be like to fall, right?
How could you know?
It's an entry into not knowing.
So maybe even better to take the backward step off.
Then you really don't know.
Then you're really trusting, right?
You're really practicing a certain kind of faith in something bigger than you, bigger than your abilities or efforts or attempts at control of some kind, attempts at setting up your life.
One thing about this, though, is I think you can't make yourself do it, and you definitely can't make somebody else do it.
That would be really bad.
You can't force this.
I think you're on the edge of your platform.
It's not like, all right, I'm going to do it!
No, one day, it's natural.
It's not a force of will kind of thing.
So maybe you do need to stay on the platform for a really long time, and maybe that's okay.
Or maybe, like in this, you're not balanced directly on the pole, sitting on the pole, so maybe that's how keenly you've cultivated your life.
A little hard on your coccyx, maybe.
You're balanced on top of a 100-foot pole.
And one day, you just find yourself stepping off, like, oh, maybe you don't even think about it.
It's just the next thing.
It's just the next thing in this life.

That's one of the things I appreciate about, when it makes sense to do requirements, whether you choose one day to do jukai or priest ordination or be shuso or something like that, is you never feel ready.
Feel ready, but when it's time to actually do it, it's like that.
It's like stepping off the pole without really thinking about it.
It's like, okay.
And then there's this feeling in your heart and in your gut, you know what I mean?
Of, like, free fall.
But it's not scary, because in that moment, you're the whole universe.
The universe is your whole body.
And we're humans, and maybe halfway down, you get all constricted and upset and worried, and we have to call 911.
Or like the one time I passed out when I was jusha during a jukai.
I don't know if anyone was here for that.
That was something.
Sometimes we freeze up, right?
We literally fall over, which I did, actually.
That was quite a scene.
So: *the man is sitting atop the 100-foot pole, on a platform, maybe.
He's gained entry, but not yet genuine.
Top the 100-foot pole, step forward.
The universe in all directions is the whole body.*
And you notice it doesn't say when you step forward.
The universe in all the directions will be the whole body.
That's already true.
It's already the space and the emptiness and the openness and not knowing.
It's already in you.
You already are that.
You are already the whole universe.
So we do our best, but we can't really do it either.
We practice.
We're patient.
We're clinging.
We're upset.
We're peaceful.
We're happy.
Oh, we have a period where we're really peaceful.
Oh, that's so nice.
But then maybe you remember that lojong slogan, don't rest in peacefulness, or something like that?
Oh, no, that's not it either.
Parked on a 100-foot pole.
So I do love, in these koans, there's often embedded quite a bit of love.
In here, love between two Dharma brothers in this deeper backstory.
Or they just appreciate each other, and then they send emissaries to check on each other.
Maybe later Master Hui thought to himself, "Oh, how nice of Brother Changsha to send that monk to check on me.
I better wander down," slipped into his room and see how he's doing.
"Maybe I'll make a little challenge, a little friendly challenge for him, too.
How are you doing, dear Dharma brother?
What have you done about the 100-foot pole?"
And you don't know where it'll lead, right?
You really don't know.
You can't know what's going to happen.
And that's one of the gifts of this strange period of COVID, right?
It's hard on us because we want to know.
We're conditioned to want to know what's going to happen, and imagine that our previous ideas of what was going to happen actually were what was going to happen, but they weren't, right?
But when the years are more similar, you can fool yourself and think, "Oh, yeah, that's right.
Just like I expected.
Now I'm on my trip to Italy."
And now you really don't know because there's no trips to Italy now.
So we don't know what's going to happen with each of us.
We don't know what's going to happen with our town, our nation, our world.
We don't know what's going to happen with our environment and whether these terrible fires will continue to get worse every year.
The whole universe stepped off the 100-foot pole.
I'm sure there's a lot of things we could have done better.
Al Gore thinks we had some big opportunities because we shifted the whole thing, but we didn't.
We were clinging to our comfortable platform as a society and going to the gas station.
But these old masters are still there.
These old masters are still whispering to us, reminding us that it's not the way you think it is.
It's not going to happen this way or that way.
There's more.
There's more.
You made an entry, but you're not yet genuine.
You're balanced on the pole, and now it's time to step off.
So we don't know what's next for Red Cedar Zen with no physical home, and I'm enjoying making up fantasies about buying a beautiful building, but we don't know that's going to happen.
It actually seems possible, which is a very fun vision.
I don't know what the difference is between a vision and a fantasy exactly, right?
What's the difference?
And what's wrong with fantasy?
We had a series of homes over 29 years.
My front porch for a couple weeks in Fairhaven.
The rented rooms at the Fairhaven Library.
Nancy Welch's office for maybe about a year or so.
We met in the conference room in her office.
But being a conference room, it was full of office furniture.
There was a table we would carry out somehow.
I don't remember.
These office chairs, and there was a lot of them.
I don't think they ever had meetings where they used all those chairs.
And they were on casters, they were on wheels.
So we had this system like a fire brigade where we pushed them out and rolled them out really quickly, passed them for one person next.
It was kind of fun.
And then the first [unclear: "Armahaw"] on Unity Street, and the next one on State Street, and the third one on Forest Street, and now this strange electronic one, which was unimaginable then, right?
None of this could have been thought of then, right?
I always think of the Jetsons TV cartoon, but other than that.
So 29 years ago, starting that journey that we're continuing.
And it's the same for each of us, right?
We've each been on a journey in our life.
For me, falling off the 100-foot pole is big changes in my life, not being married anymore.
I actually got married the same year that the sitting group that Red Cedar Zen grew out of started, 29 years ago.
Jen and I got married, Bob Penny was there, and then Bob Penny and Florence Caplow and I put our heads together and said, how about a sitting group?
And we reached out to, sometime in there I reached out to Norman.
I think after the deal with [unclear: "Deed"] was done, I think I reached out to Norman and said, "Hey Norman, would it be okay if I had a sitting group?"
Which has been our pattern all along.
He's very tolerant.
He's like, "Oh sure, yeah, good idea."
He's never said to me, "You could have asked me before you did it though."
So here we are.
And I get happy giving these talks, but it's also hard.
There's sadness, and there's grief and there's fear.
Two hundred thousand people, more than all the soldiers in all the American wars, dying from a new disease, right?
This little powerful strand of RNA that knows how to replicate itself in ourselves.
We want a peaceful, happy life and yet it doesn't seem possible somehow.
And yet somehow it is.
It made me think of that wonderful poem by Katagiri Roshi, the peaceful life poem I've read that many times here.
That part in the beginning where he says, oh, it seems impossible and I despair.
Oh, someone says it is possible and I get excited.
That's paraphrasing, but the line I remember is, he says, *but whichever is chosen, it doesn't fit one's heart neatly.* So is our life possible?
Is it impossible?
Is this going to happen or that going to happen?
We believe this, we believe that.
We choose this, we choose that.
But whatever is chosen, it doesn't fit one's heart neatly.
We're balanced on top of this pole.
It's time to let go.
And it's time to live.
No matter what the circumstances.
So how's that going?
How are you living your life these days?
Are you truly here?
Are you really here in your life?

Opening your heart, listening to your suffering, trying to study and learn and practice, forgiving yourself when you screw all that up and starting again, seeking support, remembering you're in a sangha that loves you and that you'll never quite get it right.
It does not fit one's heart neatly.
And that's okay, right?
As humans, we need that little bit of edgy suffering to keep us going.
It's just our karma.
The beings in the other realms don't know how to practice.

And the way we're trying to do this together, which also is incredibly supportive and creates all these more opportunities for falling off of poles and sticking to poles and being grouchy about somebody else having a better pole than me, right?
I'm trying to be a little careful about not speaking above others, right?
And I want to just close with another poem from Master Wu Men that he offered in last week's koan.
I remember the one about the Buddha of the present and the Buddha of the future are actually serving some other master.
Who is that?
Who are they serving?
But there's always something bigger, right?
There's always something bigger than what we think, even bigger than Buddha.

Anyway, I was just remembering again Master Wu Men's comment because it's so practical for us and a good direction for us on how to step off the 100-foot pole together, in a way where we're kind and helpful to each other.
Master Wu Men wrote,
*Don't draw another's bow.
Don't ride another's horse.
Don't discuss another's faults.
Don't explore another's affairs.* *Don't draw another bow like a bow and arrow.
Don't ride another's horse.
Don't discuss another's faults.
Don't explore another's affairs.*
We're so connected, even over Zoom, weirdly enough.
Even if we never even saw each other ever again, we're so connected.
And here are all these opportunities that that connection affords.
We find a lot of bows lying around.
It's easy to draw someone else's bow, right?
And to toot someone else's horn, that would be our version of that.
Don't toot someone else's horn.
It's their horn to toot.
Don't ride someone else's horse.
It's tricky.
We wander around and we find this horse.
It's all saddled up.
It's ready to go.
It needs to be walked today.
It needs to be exercised today.
Maybe its owner forgot, got distracted.
It's too busy.
"I'll just take care of it.
I'll just take care of it."
It's not so good for us, all right?
And the third line there is exactly the, was that the sixth precept?
Don't discuss another's faults.
And then we do sometimes, right?
Thinking maybe it'll help us understand each other or be supportive.
I think we should take Master Wu Men a little more literally.
Don't discuss another's faults.
I want to work on that.
And when I screw up, I'm really sorry.
I'll keep trying to do better.
Please remind me if you notice me discussing somebody's faults.
It's pretty much not helpful.
But then this last line really provides a way to do that.
Because then you're like, "Well, I was just talking about her qualities.
It'd be helpful to explain a little bit about what I know about him."
Which is like a sneaky way of discussing another's faults.
So Master Wu Men suggests we can create an even better environment here for stepping off our poles.
Don't explore another's affairs.
And then you're like, oops, can't say it wasn't that.
So it's a trust thing, isn't it?
Trusting each other, trusting the practice, trusting each of us on our own path, even if in some way we're walking together.
Sometimes it's messy, right?
Sometimes it's harmonious and just beautiful.
Forty-something people walking slowly up Laurel Street.
Isn't that cool, the way there was all those different little sidewalks on that route?
It's kind of like amazingly perfect.
And so peaceful and quiet.
The bell's ringing, ding, ding.
The car is stopping.
People waved to us.
Of course, we're all shy people, so we were worried about holding up traffic, but they all seemed cheerful enough to see this interesting procession.
A little break from the routine.
What are they doing?
Is it Halloween already?

So Shishuang said, *When standing at the top of the 100-foot pole, one more step is necessary.* Another eminent master of old said, *You who sit at the top of the 100-foot pole, although you've entered the way, you're not yet genuine.
Proceed from the top of the pole, and you will show your whole body in the ten directions.* Or you will realize your whole body is the ten directions, is the whole universe.
There was two different translations, different sources.
Thanks for listening to all that.
Very excited.
Forty-six out of forty-eight.
But I know that I don't know that I'm going to finish.
The koans remind us of that.
Maybe I will.
